Antibody assays
Antibodies to GlyR were measured in serum and/or CSF at
Oxford University using a previously reported cell-based
assay for screening sera at 1:20 dilution (see [ 7, 8]);
binding was scored visually on a scale from 0 to 4 with [1
considered positive (see [ 8]). Serial titrations were used to
obtain quantitative values, which are reported as titers.
GAD antibides were measured in serum or CSF at SRL,
Inc. (Tokyo, Japan) with radioimmunoassay using human
recombinant GAD65. Antibodies to classical paraneoplas-
tic antigens (Hu, Ma2, amphiphysin, CRMP5) were also
measured.
To increase the number of patients with saccadic
oscillations, we subsequently added sera from nine adult
patients with OMS (four men, ﬁve females; age
27–55 years, mean 36.6 years) that had been referred to
Oxford from hospitals in the UK.
Results
The clinical details of the ﬁve patients are given in Table 1.
Cases 1, 2, and 4 are described as representative cases of
each syndrome, and the remaining two patients are
described in the Supplementary Material.
Case presentation

cases.text:
Case 1 (idiopathic PERM)
This 61-year-old woman was admitted to our hospital twice
with gait disturbance. Six weeks before admission she
began to complain of a reduced sense of taste, but not
smell. A week later she began to feel stiffness in her thigh
while walking. Two weeks before admission she became
unable to walk because of stiffness and back pain, and she
was referred to our hospital. She had no past medical
history.
On admission (March 2008) she was not able to stand
or walk because of stiffness in the lower extremities,
resulting in ﬂexion posture at the hip and knee joints in a
supine position. She also had focal spasm in the right
foot resembling ‘‘foot drop.’’ Although she had no
obvious hyperekplexia, she occasionally had myoclonic
jerks causing brief hip ﬂexion independent of sound or
tactile stimuli, which also provoked painful spasms in the
lower back. She had mildly increased tendon reﬂexes,
hyperesthesia below the Th10 dermatome, and urinary
retention. CSF showed mild pleocytosis (cells 8/ ll,
mononuclear cells 87%) and increased protein levels
(54 mg/dl). Brain, cervical, thoracic, and lumbar MRIs
were normal. Under the diagnosis of myelitis of unknown
causes, she received intravenous high-dose methylpred-
nisolone (IVMP) (1 g/day, 3 days), oral corticosteroids
(40 mg/day), and clonazepam (1 mg/day). She became
able to walk with a cane, and she was discharged 1
month after admission. Corticosteroids were tapered off
within a month.
J Neurol (2012) 259:1566–1573 1567
123
In late July 2008 she relapsed 3 months after discon-
tinuation of corticosteroids. On admission, she was alert
and cognitively intact. She had a stiff face resembling
‘‘trismus’’ and continuous contraction of the facial-cervical
muscles, causing sustained retroﬂexion of the head with
limitation of neck movements (Fig. 1). She also had
brainstem signs, including dysphagia, dysarthria, left gaze
palsy, right-gaze evoked counterclockwise rotatory nys-
tagmus, and slow saccade to the left. Doll’s eye testing did
not improve gaze palsy (Video 1a). Muscle tone was rigid
in the lower extremities (Video 1b). CSF showed a few
cells (2/ ll) and increased protein levels (52 mg/dl). Oli-
goclonal bands were detected. The brain MRI was normal.
Needle EMG demonstrated continuous muscle activities
(5–8 Hz) in the agonist and antagonist muscles in the
lower extremities. GAD antibodies were detected at high
titer in both serum (34,300 U/ml, normal \1.5) and CSF
(2,340 U/ml) (Fig. 2). She also had anti-thyroid peroxi-
dase (TPO) antibodies (1,500 U/ml, normal \0.3) and anti-
thyroglobulin (Tg) antibodies (20.2 U/ml, normal \0.3)

(Table 1). Thyroid function tests showed mild hypothy-
roidism: TSH 2.64 lIU/ml (normal 0.27–4.2), FT3 0.84
pg/ml (normal 2.2–4.4), and FT4 0.96 ng/dl (normal
1.0–1.8). Antibodies to classical paraneoplastic antigens,
including amphiphysin, were not detected.
Based on these clinical data, a diagnosis of PERM was
made. The patient began to receive IVMP (1 g/day,
5 days), followed by intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIg)
(0.4 g/kg/day, 5 days), corticosteroids (40 mg/day), bac-
lofen (30 mg/day), diazepam (6 mg/day), and clonazepam
(1 mg/day). All symptoms resolved (Video 2), and she was
discharged.
In late November 2009 when the corticosteroids were
reduced to 5 mg/day, she relapsed again. In this recurrence,
she had only right gaze palsy, ocular lateropulsion to the
left, and right-gaze evoked nystagmus without generalized
rigidity or stiffness. These eye movement abnormalities
resolved 10 days after initiation of cyclosporine (150 mg/
day) and increasing the corticosteroid dosage (20 mg/day).
Currently, she remains free of symptoms on low cortico-
steroids (10 mg/day) and cyclosporine for 20 months after
the last relapse. She had no evidence of malignancy on
extensive screening, including FDG-PET, chest and
abdominal CT scan, endoscopic examination, and mam-
mography. The disease was regarded as ‘‘idiopathic.’’

Case 2 (idiopathic OFS)
This 41-year-old woman was admitted to our hospital with
progressive oscillopsia in September 2007. Two weeks
before admission, she had a fever for 3 days. Afterwards
she developed headache and vomiting. One week before
admission, she began to develop dizziness with oscillopsia.
She was transferred to our hospital.
On admission she was alert. She had ocular ﬂutter
provoked by opening of the eyes or looking to the object.
She had no nystagmus, myoclonus, hyperreﬂexia, hyper-
ekplexia, or limb ataxia, but she was not able to walk
because of truncal ataxia. Serological tests and brain MRI
were unremarkable. CSF showed no pleocytosis (4/ ll) and
normal protein levels (30 mg/dl). Under the diagnosis of
OFS, she began to receive IVMP (1 g/day, 3 days), fol-
lowed by a gradual tapering off. All symptoms resolved.
She was discharged 3 weeks after admission. She had no
relapse for 3 years.

Case 4 (idiopathic OMS)
This 28-year-old woman was admitted to our hospital with
vertigo and head shaking in January 2009. One month
before admission she had cold-like symptoms with diar-
rhea. Three weeks before admission she developed dizzi-
ness and vomiting. Eight days before admission she
developed gait disturbance, vertigo, and oscillopsia. She
also noticed brief jerky movements of the head that were
easily provoked by sudden noise. She was admitted to this
hospital.
On admission she was alert. She had opsoclonus, truncal
ataxia, myoclonic jerks in the neck and arms, and
hyperkplexia, but no hyperreﬂexia was seen. Brain MRI
was normal. CSF showed a few white blood cells (4/ll) and
mildly elevated protein levels (49 mg/dl). She improved
after treatment with IVMP (1 g/day, 3 days), followed by
clonazepam and gradual tapering off of corticosteroids. She
was discharged 3 weeks after admission. She had no
relapse for 21 months.
Patients with OMS or OFS
In the four patients with saccadic oscillations, associated
symptoms included myoclonus, hyperreﬂexia, and hyper-
ekplexia (Table 1). Hyperekplexia was most prominent in
one patient (case 5) in whom MRI ﬂuid-attenuated inver-
sion recovery (FLAIR) images showed reversible

shown). The other patients had normal MRIs. As they all
had prodromal cold-like symptoms, without a causative
viral pathogen or systemic autoimmune disorder identiﬁed,
and showed a good response to corticosteroid therapy, their
syndromes were regarded as ‘‘idiopathic.’’

as previously reported elsewhere [ 7]). GlyR antibody titers were

This patient had three episodes of neurological manifestations in
March and late July 2008, and late November 2009. At presentation
the GlyR-antibody titer was moderate in CSF (detected at 1:25
dilution) when the patient had moderate symptoms of spinal cord
dysfunction. The antibody titer was markedly increased in CSF
(detected up to 1:125 dilution) and in serum (up to 1:900 dilution) at
the ﬁrst relapse of the disease when the patient had severe symptoms
of brainstem dysfunction with generalized stiffness. The antibody titer
decreased rapidly after treatment with high intravenous doses of
methylprednisolone (1 g/day, 5 days), intravenous immunoglobulin
(IVIg; 0.4 g/kg/day, 5 days), and oral corticosteroids (40 mg/day). At
the second relapse when the patient developed minor brainstem signs
such as left gaze palsy with gaze-evoked nystagmus, the antibody titer
was also slightly elevated. Eye movement abnormalities resolved
after initiation of cyclosporine (150 mg/day) and increasing the
dosage of corticosteroids (from 7.5–20 mg/day). The serum and CSF
GAD-antibody titer also paralleled the clinical symptoms

Antibody tests
GlyR antibodies were detected only in the patient with
PERM who also had a high titer of GAD antibodies. The
GlyR antibodies scored highly in the screening assay (score
4, positive [1) and on titration were still detectable at
1:900 in serum and 1:125 in CSF at the time of the second
hospitalization when this patient had the most prominent
symptoms. Both GAD and GlyR antibody titers paralleled
disease activity thereafter (Fig. 2). In the other four
patients with saccadic oscillations, GlyR antibodies were
not detected in their archived samples of blood or CSF
(Table 1). GlyR antibodies were also absent in the eight of
nine UK OMS patients, one patient having a value (1.5)
only just above the range of values that are found in con-
trols (0–1; median 0) [ 8]).
Discussion
GlyR antibodies have recently been described in a few
patients with variable features including striking hyper-
ekplexia, rigidity, and brainstem disturbance [ 7], and the
relationship between these antibodies and the clinical fea-
tures in different patients [ 7–10] is growing. We hypothe-
sized that GlyR antibodies could be involved in the
putative immune-mediated eye movement disorders that
are common to PERM, OMS, and OFS. GlyR antibodies
were found at high titers in one patient with PERM who did
not have hyperekplexia. This patient also had high titers of
GAD antibodies, and both GlyR and GAD antibodies
paralleled the patient’s clinical progress with marked
reductions following successful treatments (Fig. 2). GlyR
antibodies were not, however, found in four patients with
saccadic oscillations despite the fact that two of them also
had hyperekplexia. In addition, only one of nine further
patients with OMS had GlyR antibodies at a low level.
Thus, the relationship between GlyR antibodies and the
ocular motor pathophysiology of these diseases is not yet
clear.
Glycine receptors mediate inhibitory neurotransmission
in the spinal cord, brainstem, and retina [ 14]. Glycine
receptors are composed of combinations of different alpha
and beta subunits. The majority of glycinergic neurotrans-
mission in adults is mediated by heteromeric alpha1/beta
glycine receptors [ 14]. It is highly likely that the GlyR
antibodies, which bind to extracellular domains of homo-
meric alpha1 subunits [7], can reduce the numbers of GlyRs
expressed on these neurons, as recently shown for anti-
bodies to the N-methyl-
D-aspartate receptors (NMDARs)
and a-amino-3-hydroxy-5-methyl-4-isoxazolepropionic
acid receptors (AMPARs) [ 15–17]. A reduction in inhibi-
tory neuronal activity would be consistent with the clinical
syndrome, and the lack of MRI ﬁndings suggests that
inﬂammation does not play a major role in most patients.
Hyperekplexia and myoclonus are both common features of
PERM [1, 2], and they are likely due to an impairment of
central inhibitory glycinergic circuits with increased exci-
tation of spinal motoneurons [ 7]. Our results conﬁrm that
GlyR antibodies can be found at high titers in patients with
PERM, but are not necessarily associated with hyperekp-
lexia or myoclonus, which were not features of our patient
at the peak of the disease.
The features that were common to our patient with
PERM (case 1) and the ﬁrst reported case [ 7] included
generalized muscle rigidity, spasms, stiff face, and hori-
zontal-gaze palsies. In addition, our patient had a striking
stiff facial appearance because of continuous muscle con-
tractions in the lower facial and cervical muscles. The
patient’s facial appearance mimicked the ‘‘trismus’’ caused
by the toxin of Clostridium tetani [18], suggesting that
lower facial-cervical muscle spasms are likely attributed to
antibody-mediated dysfunction of glycinergic transmission
with sustained activation of lower cranial and cervical
motoneurons. Severe touch-sensitive trismus, resembling
tetanus, was also recently reported in another GlyR anti-
body-positive case [ 9], supporting our speculation.
Our patient also had eye movement abnormalities, such
as horizontal gaze palsy, gaze-evoked nystagmus, slow
saccade, and ocular lateropulsion. In Hutchinson’s case [7],
the voluntary horizontal gaze was severely impaired on
either side without gaze-evoked nystagmus. By contrast,
our patient had unilateral gaze palsy; she developed left
gaze palsy with gaze-evoked nystagmus on looking to the
right at the ﬁrst relapse, and subsequently developed right
gaze palsy with gaze-evoked nystagmus to the right and
ocular lateropulsion to the left at the second relapse. As in
the Hutchinson case [ 7], the oculocephalic reﬂex was
impaired, suggesting that gaze palsy was not due to a
supranuclear origin.
Many of these clinical features are due to focal dys-
function of the ocular motor system, suggesting that focal
areas of the brainstem can be affected in PERM. The
abducens nucleus contains abducens motoneurons and
internuclear neurons [ 13]. These neurons receive both
inhibitory glycinergic and excitatory cholinergic or gluta-
matergic signals from the neurons within the medial ves-
tibular nuclei (MVN) and nuclei prepositus hypoglossi
(NPH), which constitute the horizontal-gaze holding
network (see Supplemental Figure) [ 13]. Based on our
observation and recently reported cases [ 7–10, 19], we
speculate that GlyR antibodies may disrupt inhibitory
glycinergic signals to the abducens motoneurons and
abducens internuclear neurons. This results in a disinhibi-
tion of these neurons, causing sustained activation of ocular
motoneurons and horizontal gaze palsy (‘‘stiff eye’’).
J Neurol (2012) 259:1566–1573 1571
123
Although supranuclear gaze palsy has also been reported in
one case of SPS [ 4], the oculocephalic reﬂex could be
preserved in patients with PERM who had less severe tonic
contraction of extraocular muscles. The presence of
asymmetric gaze-evoked nystagmus, ocular lateropulsion,
and slow saccade in our patient suggests possible
involvement not only of ocular motoneurons, but also of
the horizontal gaze-holding system. Central vestibular
imbalance associated with disruption of glycinergic trans-
mission is likely to cause gaze-evoked nystagmus and
ocular lateropulsion in our patient. Further study is nec-
essary to elucidate the association between GlyR antibod-
ies and stiff eye movements, and to describe the full
spectrum of disorders associated with these antibodies
(Leite, AC; Waters, V, in preparation).
Omnipause neurons use glycine as their neurotransmit-
ter [ 20]. Omnipause neurons are considered to inhibit
tonically saccadic burst neurons. Saccadic oscillations have
traditionally been attributed to cerebellar dysfunction, but
glycinergic dysfunction of the omnipause neurons [ 11, 12],
disinhibition of the fastigial nuclei [21], and cell membrane
instability of saccadic burst neurons [ 22] have all been
proposed as hypotheses for saccadic oscillations. There-
fore, we examined GlyR antibodies in our patients with
saccadic oscillations. The absence of GlyR antibodies in
the OMS patients, in eight of nine additional sera from UK
adult OMS patients, and in ten children with either para-
neoplastic OMS or non-paraneoplastic OMS [ 23] is dis-
appointing; there must be other antibodies or immune
factors involved in this condition.
Up till now, a total of seven patients with GlyR anti-
bodies have been described [7–10, 19], but our patient with
PERM is the ﬁrst who had both antibodies to GlyR and
GAD, although a recent fatal case had GlyR and NMDAR
antibodies [19]. GAD is an intracellular protein, in contrast
to the GlyR, which is expressed on the cell surface mem-
brane. Recent experimental studies demonstrated that,
surprisingly, autoantibodies against the intracellular syn-
aptic protein amphiphysin can reduce presynaptic GAB-
Aergic inhibition after intrathecal injection into rats [ 24];
on the other hand, GAD-reactive CD4 ? T cells caused a
lethal encephalomyelitis-like disease in mice [ 25].
Although in our PERM patient, both GlyR and GAD
antibody titers paralleled the clinical disease, this may just
reﬂect the effects of the immunotherapies the patient
received. Whether GAD antibodies can cause distinct
neurological dysfunction or are a marker for additional
T cell-mediated disorders needs to be explored further,
although the good treatment response in this patient sug-
gests that the damage was not permanent. Further studies
are necessary to identify the full clinical spectrum of GlyR
antibody-mediated disease and to investigate the immu-
nopathogenic basis of all the conditions that result from
disturbance of the brainstem and spinal inhibitory
mechanisms.
